ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Construction of Jaleswar-Chandaneswar Road with world Bank Aid 
*61 DR. M.N. DAS: Will the Minister of SURFACE TRANSPORT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the World Bank has un dertaken the 
construction of a 30 km. road from Jaleswar to Chandaneswar in Orissa for 
which there has been constant popular demand for years; and 
(b) if so, by when the construction work is likely to begin? 
THE MINISTER OF SURFACE TRANSPORT (SHRI FlAJNATH 
SINGH): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
DR. M.N. DAS: Sir, with a clear conscience and in total comfidcncc let 
me say, with due apology, that the hon. Minister has noi consulted the papers 
in regard to this or has not taken into confidence   the   concerned   officers   
or   has   not   called   for   the 
inforrmation from the Government of Orissa. 
 
 We have been told a number of times that work on the road from Jaleswar to 
Chandaneswar will begin from the coming September, 2000. As I wanted to 
spend money out of my MPLADS funds to repair the road, I was warned by 
the Administration of Orissa that no renovation work and no repair work 
could be undertaken because already the World Bank project was to start 
from September this year. I do not know whether the Gov ernment has 
obtained the papers in regard to all these things. That, of course, is a 
different issue.

RAJYA SABHA           [29th February, 2000] 
Sir, there may be hundreds of stretched of 30 kilometre road which are in a 
very poor condition, but the re ason why I am referring to this particular road 
is this. My esteemed friends to my left coming from West Bengal and 
belonging to different parties know a place named Digha. They must have 
visited Digha sevral times, which the late lamented Dr. Bidhan Chand ra Roy, 
the first Congress Chief Minister of West Bengal, made into a health resort. It 
is on a beach on the Bay of Bengal. Every day, thousands of tourists go there. 
It is a thriving centre of tourism. Within one to two kilometers from Digha i.s 
the Orissa Border and thousands of tourists, who go to Digha, make it a point 
to cover just half -a-kilometre inside Orissa to go to a place of pilgrimage 
named Chandaneswar. That is another thing. But my point is that, hundreds of 
heavily loaded trucks start from C alcutta every day to come to Digha because 
the road is very good from Calcutta to Digha. They enter into Orissa and 
come to Chandaneswar. From there they take the only rural road to Jaleswar. 
Sir, heavily loaded trucks constantly passing through that stret ch day and 
night in hundreds are making the road totally impassable for the movement of 
vehicles. Local buses cannot ply. There are big holes and craters. As a result, 
the vehicles get badly damaged. That is why the people have been constantly 
demanding for a good State highway. I have been told by the Government of 
Orissa that the World Bank has already sanctioned Rs. 9'' - crores to construct 
that 30 -kilometre stretch. There is a constant pressure on me that a,5 a 
Member of Parliament, I should spend money on it from out of -the MPLADS 
to get the road repaired. But when I asked the Collector of my district, 
Balasore, to spend Rs. 50 lakhs from out of \  the MPLADS funds for the 
repair of the road so that at least the cyc.\ist? can cross that stretch of road and 
also the local buses can ply, I wa \s told that since the World Bank work 
would begin in September 2000," no renovation or repair work could be 
undertaken from out of the MPLADS funds or from any other source, not 
even from the funds of the Public Works  Department of the Government of 
Orissa. 
Now, how does the hon. Minister say that there is no such project and the 
question does not arise? Sir, if I am permitted, in due course

DR. M.N. DAS: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I want to have one information from 
the hon. Minister. Is he aware of the fact that if a road from Jaleswar to 
Chandanesar, a stretch of only 30 KMs, is constructed, the  heavy vehicular 
traffic from Calcutta towards the far South, passing through Orissa on 
National Highway will be reduced by a distance of 170 KMs? The National 
Highway from Calcutta to Chennai runs through a circuitous route, touching 
the Bihar border and entering Balasore, Orissa. If this stretch of 30 KMs 
road is constructed, the distance could be shortened by 170 Kms. Is the 
Government aware of that fact? Why is the Government not giving priority 
to the construction of this road? That is my humble submission.

(vi) DoT did not charge the one time entry fee from the existing licensees

hug($ revenue loss to the Government, difficult to be assessed at this stage in

(vii) Cellular licensees did not pay WPC (Wireless Planning and

31.5.1999.   N o   separate   WPC   license   was   signed   with   cellular 
licensees. 
(viii) Government issued the offer of migration in a hurried manner and is 
fraught with the serious risk of frauds etc. 
(ix) Extension in the license period by 5 —10 years has been granted 
without linking such extension with their performance. Thus, losing 
opportunity of not granting extension to defaulting licensees for not 
discharging their contractual obligations or failing to provide

(x) The migration p ackage was offered on the basis of the advice of

apprehensions were expressed by expert Group on Telecommunications 
(GoT). The financial advice regarding probable effect on the contracted 
parties is not within the scope of legal advice and therefore, any decision 
taken on this basis is not sound unless supported by advice of expert 
financial body. 
Statement-II 
Any loss of revenue would have to be seen in a complete context. A brief 
background of the licensing scheme is as below: 
(i) In consideration of totality of circumstances, the Government took a 
decision to allow migration of existing licensees of Basic and Cellular 
Services to NTP -99 regime of revenue sharing from a prospective date of 
1.8.1999. The licence fee dues upto the cut -off date of 31.7.1999 as per the 
existing license agreement and af ter marking adjustments towards notional 
extension of effective date in terms of migration package, were payable by 
the hcensees. 
(ii) There is no reduction as such in the amount of arrears in terms of the 
package offered to existing licensees for migratio n to NTP -99 regime of 
revenue sharing. The rate of interest and its penal nature remain intact. The 
only relief provided is by way of across the board extension of effective date 
by six months (subject to the condition 
61 

RAJYA SABHA               [29th February, 2000] 
that any extension granted earlier was accounted for) in consideration of the 
delays in granting clearances etc. which led to a spate of htigation. It 
involved a reduction of Rs. 1443.58 crores in receipt of licence fee on this 
count. It may be highlighted that this relief of extension of effective date has 
not been granted to the Metro Cellular Operators because they were placed in 
a comparatively favourable position. 
Justification of Migration Policy: 
* Existing licensees under the 1994 Polic y enjoy the right to operate their 
licenses under duopoly arrangement [with DoT/ MTNL (Mahanagar 
Telephone Nigam Limited) as the third operator in Cellular Services]. 
Upon their migration to NTP-99 regime on acceptance of the conditions 
of migration as a p ackage, these existing licensees will forego the 
duopoly arrangement and will have to operate under the multipoly 
arrangement as provided in the NTP-99. 
* It is open to the Government to change the policy, if it is considered 
that such a policy would be conducive to the revival of the telecom 
Industry and the interests of the general public will be better served by 
providing services to a large segment of the population at affordable 
rates. 
* The changes in the Information and Communication Tech nology have 
been so fast and swift that the events have over taken the policy 
objectives and framework of the 1994 Telecom Policy. 
* With the services being made more affordable, the consumer base is 
bound to substantially increase and the license^ regime which involves 
sharing of revenue would yield substantial sums to the Government as 
revenue share. Needless to mention that an independent body, viz., 
TRAI would regulate the rental chargeable from the consumers, thus 
taking care of consumer interest. 
* There were enormous a mount of litigation between the Licensees and 
the Licensor before the TRAI, and before the 
62 

[29th February, 2000]            RAJYA SABHA 
High Court. Claims were also initiated by way of arbitration. It would 
not contribute to public interest to perpetua te such Htigious regime. 
The Government has taken into account this aspect as well as other 
facts referred to here- in-above and envolved the package in larger 
public interest. 
Other details giving an overview of the problems of the existing licensees 
under old policy framework, the new policy framework of NTP -99, 
Government decision on migration policy and benefits of the migration 
policy are enclosed as Annexure-III. 
Statenient-III 
(i) Background—Problems of existing licensees under old policy 
framework: 
Though the selection of Licensees was through open bids, the design of 
the license fee structure has not proved conducive to growth of services in 
subsequent years. 
High bids particularly for the Cellular Circles and Basic Services were 
made in the hope of large growth of business which has not come true. 
Service providers as well as their Associations had been requesting for 
several reliefs like moratorium on licence fee payment, extension of the 
period -of license, extension of effective date etc. on the g rounds of their 
alleged precarious financial condition. Delays in clearance by various 
authorities, governmental bodies and agencies were also cited as reasons for 
seeking reliefs. 
Defaults were committed by the licensees in the due payment of license 
fee. Payments were not coming through and arrears were mounting. Efforts 
to encash the bank guarantees were stayed by the Court.vTciccom 
Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) as a result of large number of legal 
proceedings initiated by licen.secs. 
The licensing framework of the 1994 Telecom Policy did not achieve its 
objectives. Large capital resources were invested by the private licensees in 
the telecom sector and their non-viability was 
63 

RAJYA SABHA           [29th February, 2000] 
affecting the domestic a nd foreign financial institutions funding the projects. 
This in turn was affecting the viability of the telecom service industry itself. 
(ii) The New Policy frame work of New Telecom Policy- 1999 (NTP —
1999) 
Government therefore constituted a high level 'Gro up on Telecom' (GoT) 
to recommend New Telecom Policy and also to consider problems of 
existing Hcensees under the new policy framework. The NTP -99 
recommended by the GoT was approved by the Government effective from 
1.4.1999. 
The NTP -99 has been widely accepted as an improvement upon the 
previous policy and is seen as a step in the right direction meeting the 
imperatives of technological developments, market growth and national 
interest. Shift from payment of fixed license fees to revenue sharing in the 
multipoly situation which was recommended by GoT has been accepted by 
the Government. The objective of the NTP -99 is to activate investments and 
competition in the telecom sector; its thrust is to create a modern and 
efficient telecommunications infrastructur e taking into account the 
convergence of Information Technology (IT), media, telecom and consumer 
electronics and thereby propel India into becoming an IT superpower. In that 
context requiring the existing license holders to function and continue under 
the 1994 Policy concurrently with NTP -99, without extending to them the 
migration to NTP -1999 would have led to serious anomalies. This would be 
impracticable in a market economy structure in a multipoly competitive 
license regime. 
NTP-99 also announced the G overnment's intention to satisfactorily 
resolve the problems being faced by the existing operators in a manner which 
is consistent with the contractual obligations and is legally tenable. 
(Hi) Government decision on Migration Policy: 
While approving the Ne w Telecom Policy, it was noted, inter -alia, that it 
is in the public interest for the New Telecom Policy to be uniformly    
applicable    all    over   the    country; ,the    Government 
64 

[29th February, 2000]                RAJYA SABHA 
accordingly deci ded that the advice of the Attorney General be obtained, 
inter-alia, on the issue as to whether it is legally possible to bring the 
existing licensees under the New Telecom Policy regime and if so, the 
appropriate modalities therefor. 
After taking into consideration all relevant material and submissions made 
before GoT, inter -alia, by Financial Institutions (FIs), representations 
received from operators; Government arrived at a considered decision that 
having regard to the ground realities and the prevailin g situation facing the 
telecom industry, migration of licensees from the 1994 Telecom Policy to 
NTP-99 regime was warranted and integration of existing licensees into 
NTP-99 not retrospectively but prospectively, would be in over all public 
interest. 
On consideration of the legal opinion given by the Attorney General and 
views of FIs and consideration of all relevant facts including possible 
implications, the Government decided (July 6, 1999) in favour of the 
migration package which combines the twin benefi ts of having a uniform 
licensing poicy in the whole country as also resolving the problems of the 
existing licensees in a manner which is legally sound. 
(iv) Benefits of Migration Policy: 
Strict enforcement of the Hcense conditions would have in many cases  
lead to serious financial losses, if not bankruptcy. Many large Indian 
companies already in the field, would have shut down operations and there 
would have been disruption of this vital segment of the communication 
services. Government took the view that this would not be conducive to 
public interest. Any termination of the licenses would have had an immediate 
dampening effect on the banks and financial institutions, both national and 
international and could well result in lack of lenders and investors con fidence 
in the Indian Telecom Sector. Banks which had furnished Bank Guarantees 
may not be able to recover the guaranteed sums from the guarantors, viz.; the 
operators. This would also have an adverse impact on the financial health of 
the banking institutions. 
In the emerging scenario, telecom tariffs (to be determined by 
65 

RAJYA SABHA             [29th February, 2000] 
TRAI) are going to be progressively reduced. On this account, no problems 
are likely to be faced under the licensing fee structure of NTP -99 which 
provides for payment of licence fee in the form of revenue share (as against 
the earlier fixed licence fee structure). 
The downward tariff trends, would also benefit the consumer, push 
demand for telephones in the rural areas and thus effectively serve the 
objective of improving tele -density and rural penetration under NTP -99 
regime. 
Termination of Ucenses, and invocation of Bank Guarantees would lead to 
immediate and long drawn out litigation by current licensees. On the other 
hand, the new revenue sharing regime in NTP -99 would enhance competition 
by bringing in multiple operators, giving them flexibility to adjust in future to 
fast changing technologies and tariff changes, lead to induction of more 
number of players in the field and offer lower t ariffs and better quality of 
service to the consumer. Once the growth of the sector is ensured, the revenue 
streams will also be more healthy and the Government will be in a better 
position to realize revenues due to it. Public interest would, therefore, b e 
better served if the existing licensees were allowed to migrate to the New 
Telecom Policy-1999 regime. 
The uniform application of NTP -99 all over the country would ensure 
growth of telecom sector which is a vehicle for information technology and 
will fulfil the vision of India, to be an IT superpower.

Recommendations of the Committees Set up by RBI and action taken 
thereon 
1. Working Group on NGOs and SHGs 
With a view to studying the functioning of SHGs and NGOs for expanding 
their activities and deepening their role in the rural sector, the Governor, RBI 
had in November 1994 constituted a Working Group comprising eminent 
NGO functionaries, academicians, consultants and bankers under the 
Chairmanship of Shri S.K. Kalia, Managing Director, NABARD. The 
members of the Working Gr oup visited a number of NGOs and SHGs, held 
widespread discussions and studied several issues concerning SHGs and 
NGOs through a sample of 171 SHGs 49 NGOs and 97 bank branches. The 
recommendations of the Working Group are as under. 
The Working Group was o f the view that the linking of SHGs with the 
banks is a cost effective, transparent and flexible approach to improve the 
accessibility of credit from the formal banking system to 
96 

[29th February, 2000]               RAJYA SABHA 
the unreached rural poor.  It is expected to offer the much -needed solution to 
the twin problems being faced by the banks, viz. Recovery of loan in the 
rural areas and the high transaction cost in dealing with small borrowers at 
frequent intervals. The Group, therefore, felt that t he thrust of the policy 
should be to encourage the formation of SHGs and their linking with the 
banks and in this regard, the banks have a major role to play. The Group has 
recommended inter-alia, that the banks treat the linkage programme as a 
business opportunity for reaching the rural poor and making it a part of their 
corporate strategy, the programme be made a part of Service Area Approach 
and LBR reporting system and regular training curriculum of banks, lending 
of banks to SHGs being made a separate segment under the priority sector, 
introducing review and monitoring of SHGs linkage programme,  etc. 
Simultaneously, the Group has suggested for capacity building of NGOs, 
training of their staff, etc. 
2. High Level Committee on Agricultural Credit through Commercial Banks 
A Committee (Chairman: Shri R.V. Gupta) constituted by the Reserve 
Bank in December 1997 to review and examine the issties on agricultural 
credit and to suggest measures that would give an impetus to the flow of 
credit to this sector sub mitted its report in April 1998. The major 
recommendations of the Committee accepted by the Reserve Bank are 
highlighted below. 
• simplification of procedures regarding loan application forms, 
agrements/documents etc; 
• rationalisation of internal returns of banks; 
• introduction of a comprehensive cash credit limits to agricultural 
farmers; 
• introduction of new loan products with savings components; 
• cash disbursement of loan, dispensation of no due certificates, discretion 
to banks on matters relating to margin/s ecurity requirements for 
agricultural loans above Rs. 10,000; 
• delegating powers to branch managers; and 
97 

RAJYA SABHA.           [29th February, 2000] 
addressing a host of HRD related issues with regard to bank officials 
posted at rural branches. 
The com mittee's recommendations relating to most of the procedural 
modifications have been implemented by banks and it is expected that the 
procedural improvements will lead to a substantial reduction in paper work 
and simplify the delivery mechanism for flow of credit to farmers.

BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) As per the Guidelines for Indian

other authority in the area where the applicant proposes to practise as Notary, 
the objections, if any, to the appointment of the applicant as Notary. The 
applicant is also given an  opportunity  of  hearing  again.st   the  objections,   
if  any.   After

588. SHRIMATI KAMLA SINHA: Will the Minister of WATER

such report has been received from the Washington -based World Watch 
Institute. However, on an average the water availabilit y in the country 
remains more or less fixed accounting to the natural hydrologic cycle. The

population. The average per capita yearly water availability which is 
estimated to be ab out 1900 Cu. m. in 2000 AD may come down to 1350 Cu.

criteria any situation of yearly water availability less than 1000 Cu. m. per 
capita is considered as scarcity condition. Therefore, even by the end of 2025

Effectiveness of Dams to Control Flood 
599. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any detailed study to ascertain the 
effectiveness of dams to control flood; and 
(b) if so, the salient points made and conclusion raised in the study? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) 
Government of India constituted in July, 1976 Rashtriya Barh Ayog (RBA) to 
examine and advise on various aspects relating to floods. The RBA 
considered inter-alia the aspects of effectiveness of the dam/reservoirs to 
control flood. The salient points / views / conclusions as brought out by RBA 
in their report of 1980 on this issue is as under: 
"Reservoirs in general even without specific flood storage space, 
187 

RAJYA SABHA              [29th February, 2000] 
have a beneficial effect on the flood problems of a basin. The effectiveness 
of reservoirs in moderating floods would depend upon the capacity available 
for absorbing flood runoff. Because of their high cost, reservoirs may well be 
justified for direct benefits like water supply, irrigation and hydro -electric 
power generation, but are likely to be uneconomical if. constructed 
exclusively for flood moderation. It is, therefore, good practice t o construct 
multi-purpose reservoirs with flood moderation as one of the functions, 
instead solely for flood moderation. 
Compared to other physical measures, reservoirs take a longer period for 
their investigation and execution. Also quite often, the avail able sites for 
reservoirs are remote from the areas where flood damages occur, whereas 
their flood moderation impact decreases with distance. On the other hand, 
under favourable conditions, reservoirs are a dependable measure, which, by 
itself or in combin ation with other measures can considerably mitigate the 
flood problem of a river basin. Reservoirs to the extent technically and 
economically feasible, must be considered as an important component in any 
package of measures for flood management." 
Finally in the Chapter entitled "Summary of Recommendations" the RBA 
in one of their recommendations has suggested as under:—  
"Flood space should be provided in reservoirs after examining the need 
feasibility."

SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMl (Nominated): Sir, I rise to express my 
deep anguish at the manner in which the Indian Council of Historical Research 
has chosen to withdr aw two volumes of the prestigious "Towards Freedom" 
series by Prof. Sum it Sarkar and Prof. K. N. Panikkar, directly from the Oxford 
University Press bypassing the General Editor, Prof. S. Gopal. Such blatant 
interference in the editorial sanctity of a maj or academic project cannot augur 
well for this nation. The I.C.H.R. did not observe even the minimum propriety 
of informing the authors about its decision. Both, Prof Panikkar and Prof. 
Sumit Sarkar, are distinguished historians, who have consistently uphe ld 
secular and progressive values in their approach to history.   By this action of 
withdrawal, the I.C.H.R. has 
194 

[29th February, 2000]                RAJYA SABHA 
shown utter disregard for the autonomy of an academic institution and it has 
shown contem pt for independent research. When Prof. Sarkar and Prof. 
Paniickar were entrusted with this project in 1989, thereby, nailing the lie that 
it has taken 27 years to complete this project, it was under a specific 
understanding that they would be answerable only to the general editor, 
Professor S. Gopal, both in form and in content and that is why they took up 
this project. Now, by imposition of an External Review Committee, the fact 
that their independence and their autonomy has been violated is clearly 
established. It is a great pity that the I.C.H.R. is now manned by people who 
are insensitive to the academic implications of autonomy being violated. It is a 
real pity. It has also to be seen as a part of the larger scenario that is 
happening in the country. I t is an attempt by the Sangh Pariwar to impose its 
own ideology in matters of social, cultural and academic issues. It is 
becoming completely clear that it, is the writ of the Sangh Pariwar rather than 
any institutional norms that are at play. Coupled with these are a whole series 
of allegations that are also being made and are confusing the subject. It is 
being said that crores of rupees have been spent; it has taken 27 years to 
complete the project, etc. But, the fact is, the editors are to receive an 
Honourarim of Rs.25,000/ - after completion of the project. Any money that 
has spent so far, has been directely spent by the Council for its research, 
assistants and it has got nothing to do with the editors I have already stated 
that the editors came into pic ture only in 1989 and so. it has not taken these 
many years that they are talking about. 
It is also being said that what is done now has a precedent. It is said 
that Shri P.N. Chopra's volume was similarly reviewed by the then Chairman 
of the I.C.H.R. and the volumes edited by him were withdrawn. The fact is, the 
present proposal review has no similariity with that of the past. Shri P.N. 
Chopra was direct employee of the I.C.H.R. and conditions were that he was 
answerable to the Chairman. Whereas, in the pr esent case, the two people 
were answerable only to Professor Gopal and his autonomy has been 
violated. The mala fide intention is obvious from the very constitution of the 
Review Committee. Volumes dociimenting the history of the freedom 
movement require not only a general expertise on modern Indian history, but 
also a deep understanding of archival and non-official matters. The Review 
Committee does not have people of thisexpertise. It has a retired bureaucrat, 
a historian of ancient India, and an archaeologist.

In the light of the above, we demand that severe action be taken 
against the ICHR Chairman for violating all academic norms. The alliance 
partners of the NDA, committed, as they are, to the princi ples of secularism, 
must stand up and be counted. They need to defeat the designs of the Sangh 
Parivar and the RIP and its hidden agenda and insist that educational 
institutions should not be allowed to fall a prey to any given particular 
dispensation, or be allowed to adulterate history, or suppress genuine 
historical writings. 
There is a general impression in the hindutava camp that the 
volumes under discussion, being documented history, might contain 
incontrovertible evidence about the collaboration of H indu communal forces 
with colonialism. That is likely to damage for ever the possible projection of the 
RSS leaders as freedom fighters. Discrediting the authors of these volumes 
and preventing their publication is rooted in this political logic. What is 
happening to "Towards Freedom" is not an isolated instance. It is part of a 
larger design of the Sangh Parivar to transform India into a Hindu nation. The 
disruption of the shooting of 'Water', the blackening of the face of a school 
teacher in Goa, and the intimidation of citizens in Lucknow and Kanpur are 
unmistakable forebodings of India's plurality under fire. The withdrawal of 
these volumes has to be located in the larger context.
